perspective:
Harold’s available information, from his own perspective:

- He is a project manager, feels frustrated/anxious about his project’s progress, and believes his team is unmotivated. He arranges and attends a coffee-shop meeting with his trusted friend/advisor Arthur.
- At that meeting, he hears Arthur say motivation can be tricky and ask whether Harold has tried understanding each team member’s individual drivers. Harold admits he has focused mainly on project goals/deadlines, not personal motivations. Arthur advises one-on-one conversations so people feel valued and understood. Harold agrees to try and feels more hopeful.
- Afterward, Harold feels hopeful/relieved and believes Arthur’s advice will help. He tells his team he wants one-on-one chats to understand what motivates them. He hears Team Member 1 say it could be helpful and Team Member 2 say they are open to it. Harold says he will schedule time and wants them to make the project succeed together.
- Later, Harold observes the team still is not responding well. He feels disappointed/worried and tells Arthur he tried the suggestions. Arthur suggests deeper issues may be at play, such as personal conflicts, lack of trust, or external stressors. Harold says he will set up another round of meetings to investigate.
- Feeling determined/focused, Harold believes there may be unaddressed underlying team issues. In one-on-one meetings, he asks team members for concerns. Team Member 1 tells him there is tension among a few people affecting work. Harold says he will look into resolving conflicts. Team Member 2 tells him they feel overwhelmed by workload and stressed. Harold says he understands and will see about redistributing tasks, because their well-being matters.
- Feeling optimistic/empowered, Harold believes addressing individual concerns will improve performance. He tells the team he will add regular feedback sessions and team-building activities to create a more supportive environment. Team Member 1 says it sounds great and helpful; Team Member 2 agrees their concerns are being addressed. Harold says he is glad and emphasizes that their input and well-being are crucial.

He does not have access to private/internal thoughts of Arthur or the team members, narrator-only character traits, or hidden team dynamics beyond what he observed or was told.
